CLAUDE.md

Source: CLAUDE.md

This file provides guidance to Claude Code (claude.ai/code) when working with code in this repository.

What this is

zuint gives R lossless wide integer vectors, int64, uint64, int128 and uint128, so that every integer type Arrow and DuckDB produce survives the trip into R and back with its schema and values intact. All four types share one C core and one promotion lattice. int64 keeps the bit64 integer64 layout so existing consumers read it unchanged, and within that layout it is a stricter second implementation: exact or explicit, overflow as a policy, summaries in the right type (design §0.1). Dependencies outside the zu-* family are allowed only in Suggests (design §2.1): zufast (>= 0.1.1) is LinkingTo only, R (>= 4.3.0) is required for chooseOpsMethod(), and bit64, nanoarrow, arrow, duckdb, vctrs, pillar and gmp are Suggests used in tests and lazily registered methods. It does not fork bit64, do arithmetic on small integer types, offer arbitrary precision, handle decimals (the companion decimal package does, and depends on zuint, never the reverse), or do matrix algebra.

The specification is .agents/design.md, adopted from RFC 0009. It outranks this file: CLAUDE.md orients, the design doc decides.

Current state

Scaffolded 2026-10-15 with create-pkg.sh; no functionality yet. The roadmap in .agents/roadmap.md takes it to v0.1.0. The design’s milestones number versions differently (its first CRAN release is “v0.3”); the roadmap maps them onto 0.1.0.

Stage tracking

Progress toward the next version is tracked as GitHub sub-issues, so the parent issue shows a progress bar such as “6 of 7”.

  • One parent issue per target version, titled with the bare version, for example v0.1.0. v0.1.0 issue: created by pkg-roadmap.
  • One sub-issue per roadmap stage, titled as the roadmap titles it, for example Stage 3 — R interface, and linking to that section. The number of stages is whatever the roadmap has; there is no fixed scale.
  • Every tracking issue carries the stage label, so it can be told apart from bug and feature issues and left out of open-issue counts.
  • Close a stage by merging its pull request. Put Closes #<n> in the body of the stage’s pull request. Never close a stage whose exit criteria are not met; record a deviation in the roadmap first.
  • The roadmap stays authoritative. The issues record which stages are done, not what a stage requires. Adding, removing or renaming a stage means editing the roadmap and the sub-issues in the same change.
  • Each stage has a CI tier, quick or full. The roadmap sets it, and quick is the default. See Continuous integration for what each means. The second-to-last stage, Full CI, runs the full set and fixes what it finds before v0.1.0 readiness.
  • Close the parent issue when CRAN accepts the version and it is tagged. Opening a parent issue implies at least one stage sub-issue; a parent with no sub-issues shows no progress on the board.

Versioning

A new package develops at 0.0.0.9000 and targets 0.1.0 for its first CRAN release. Set Version: 0.1.0 and the matching NEWS.md heading when the package enters Pre-flight. Bump to 0.1.0.9000 only after CRAN accepts it, never before: a .9000 version above an unreleased 0.1.0 heading is wrong.

Until the first release the R API may change freely. Sibling packages can still depend on this one before CRAN does, through Remotes: or LinkingTo:. A package that others wait on should reach CRAN first.

zuint itself waits on zufast: the 128-bit primitives come from its wide.h header, so zufast (>= 0.1.1) must be on CRAN before zuint is submitted. Until then development builds against zufast’s dev version: DESCRIPTION has LinkingTo: zufast (>= 0.1.0.9000) and Remotes: pedrobtz/zufast. When zufast 0.1.1 is released, raise the constraint to >= 0.1.1 and delete Remotes: in the same commit. CRAN rejects a Remotes: field, so this is part of entering Pre-flight.

Commands

Run from the package root.

Rscript -e 'devtools::load_all()'                # compile src/ and load
Rscript -e 'devtools::document()'                # roxygen -> NAMESPACE, man/
Rscript -e 'devtools::test()'                    # full testthat suite
Rscript -e 'devtools::test(filter = "<name>")'   # one test file
Rscript -e 'devtools::test(shuffle = TRUE)'      # order independence
Rscript -e 'devtools::check()'                   # R CMD check
air format .                                     # format R sources

The fallback for compilers without __int128 is built by setting ZUINT_CPPFLAGS=-DZUF_NO_INT128 in the environment, which src/Makevars passes to the compiler. Clean the old objects first, and set ZUINT_EXPECT_INT128=false so test-storage.R confirms the fallback really was built:

Rscript -e 'devtools::clean_dll()'
ZUINT_CPPFLAGS=-DZUF_NO_INT128 ZUINT_EXPECT_INT128=false \
  Rscript -e 'devtools::test()'
Rscript -e 'devtools::clean_dll()'               # back to the native build

CI runs this as the no-int128 job of R-CMD-check.yaml, on every pull request.

Architecture

Grows with the stages; .agents/design.md §10 has the planned C layout.

  • src/zu_wide.h is the type layer: the type codes, the NA sentinels, raw word access to the REALSXP and CPLXSXP payloads, and zu_val, a sign plus a 128-bit magnitude that slow paths use to move a value between types with one range check (zu_val_fits()).
  • src/zu_cast.c holds construction and conversion. Entry points that can lose a value return list(result, n_lost) and R raises the warning, so condition classes live only in R.
  • R/types.R has the constructors, the NA_*_ constants and zu_storage(); R/cast.R is the one conversion path every method uses; R/conditions.R lists the condition classes.
  • R/vector.R holds the base vector methods, written once and registered for all four classes from the zu_methods table through @evalNamespace. To add a method, add it to that table.

Invariants that are easy to break

  • int64 keeps the bit64 layout: a REALSXP whose bits are int64_t, class c("zu_int64", "integer64"). data.table, arrow, duckdb and others read REAL(x) as int64_t*; any other layout breaks them silently.

  • Never register methods on bare integer64, only on zu_* classes. Otherwise zuint changes bit64’s behaviour for everyone who loads it.

  • Every method bit64 defines for integer64, zuint defines for zu_int64. A missing one falls through to bit64’s method when bit64 is loaded and to base R on the raw bits when it is not, so the answer would depend on what else is attached.

  • chooseOpsMethod() must return TRUE for every zu_* class. Without it, zu_int64 + integer64 warns “incompatible methods” and R does double arithmetic on the bits. This is why R (>= 4.3.0).

  • 128-bit values cross the Arrow bridge as the arrow.opaque hugeint/uhugeint extension, not as decimal128(38, 0): DuckDB reads the decimal back as DECIMAL, and the decimal form reads UHUGEINT ≥ 2¹²⁷ as negative (design §9.1).

  • 128-bit arithmetic comes from zufast/wide.h, not from code written here. zu_ops.h holds only the NA and overflow-policy layer, so zuint and zutempo share one implementation. The portable fallback (ZUF_NO_INT128) must keep building.

  • Signed overflow must never reach C undefined behaviour. Check before the operation, using the checked or wrapping primitives.

  • Mixed-type operations are lossless or an error, following the promotion lattice in design §5. Never coerce through double.

  • Base R pads with its own NA, which is a valid value here. x[i] past the end, x[i] <- v past the end and length<- fill with NA_real_ or NA_complex_, whose bits are an ordinary int64 or int128. The methods in R/vector.R find the padded positions and write the type’s sentinel; any new method that can grow a vector must do the same.

  • Bits move between doubles and integers by memcpy only. A cast through double would canonicalise the NaN payloads that negative int64 values and the unsigned NAs occupy.

  • The NA_*_ constants are built in pure R at install time, from bit patterns (-0 is INT64_MIN), because the shared object is not loaded when the package’s R code is evaluated.

  • Native routines are called through their registered symbols. init.c calls R_forceSymbols(), so .Call("name", ...) with a string fails; use the symbol useDynLib(.registration = TRUE) defines.

Add each new one when a stage establishes it.

Testing conventions

  • Self-sufficient. Every test builds its own inputs inside the test_that() block. No file-scope objects.
  • Self-contained. Global state goes through withr::local_*(), randomised input through withr::local_seed(). Tests write only under tempdir().
  • Assert on condition classes, never message text. Use expect_error(..., class = "<pkg>_<kind>_error"). Wording belongs in snapshot tests.
  • Order independence. devtools::test(shuffle = TRUE) is part of the definition of done.
  • Borrow a conformance suite before writing one. Mainstream implementations in Python, Java, Go or Node usually ship a test corpus. Use it as an oracle rather than inventing cases by hand. gmp is the oracle for values (helper-oracle.R); the DuckDB/Arrow/Parquet round-trip matrix, the acceptance test, arrives in Stage 5.
  • Run the int64 tests with and without bit64 attached. Any difference means a method is missing on zu_int64 (see Invariants). The bit64-attached run also covers mixed zu_int64 ⊕ integer64 dispatch.
  • Helpers live in tests/testthat/helper-*.R. helper-oracle.R gives each type’s range, edge values, out-of-range values and random fills, computed with gmp (and skips without it). helper-bit64.R runs a string of R code in two fresh Rscript processes, one with bit64 attached and one where it never loaded, because S3 methods stay registered once a namespace has loaded; it skips on CRAN.
  • Keep the suite inside the CRAN time budget. About 5 seconds locally (2026-10-16), most of it the two bit64 processes.

Definition of done

devtools::document() and devtools::check() clean, meaning 0 errors, 0 warnings and 0 notes. The one allowed note is “New submission” before the first release. devtools::test(shuffle = TRUE) green. CI green at the change’s tier: the quick profile for a quick roadmap stage or an ordinary pull request, the full profile for a full stage, Full CI, and every release. A user-facing change also needs a test, roxygen documentation and a NEWS.md entry.

Releasing to CRAN

  • CI is the pre-submission check. The pedrobtz/r-actions R CMD check runs --as-cran on the CRAN-like runners and containers, and it replaces win-builder, the macOS builder and R-hub. None of them is a release step, and cran-comments.md lists the CI legs as its test environments.
  • Entering Pre-flight. The roadmap’s feature stages are done, the version is set as in Versioning, NEWS.md and cran-comments.md are written, and CI is green. Only submission work remains.
  • Before submitting, run the cran-extrachecks and review-cran-submission skills, and resolve every finding.
  • The pretest is automated and does not read cran-comments.md. A NOTE that is explained but not fixed gets the upload archived. Fix the NOTE, as under Vendored native code, instead of justifying it.
  • After acceptance, tag v0.1.0, publish the GitHub release, bump to 0.1.0.9000, and close the version’s parent issue.

Editing rules

  • roxygen comments are the source. Never edit man/ or NAMESPACE by hand.
  • Edit README.Rmd, not the generated README.md.
  • Keep prose simple and short. One idea per sentence.
  • Wrap roxygen text at 80 characters and run air format . on R sources.
  • Use lower_snake_case, and prefix internal native symbols with <pkg>_.
  • Keep hard runtime dependencies at zero unless a recorded design decision says otherwise.
  • Export and document public functions. Do not create roxygen topics for internal ones.

Continuous integration

Workflows come from pedrobtz/r-actions. Call those reusable workflows instead of writing bespoke ones, and pin a released tag rather than main. Pin a workflow that holds a write token, such as coverage.yml, to a commit, with the tag in a comment. The R-CMD-check workflow must call r-cmd-check.yml, because a hand-rolled one does not count as the pre-submission check.

This package calls r-cmd-check.yml@v1 with nosuggests and nold on (from R-CMD-check.yaml); valgrind.yml, lto.yml, gctorture.yml, rchk.yml, analyzers.yml and cran-special.yml (from native-checks.yml); and coverage.yml, pinned to the v1 commit, with its badge on gh-pages because main takes no direct pushes (from coverage.yaml). pkgdown.yaml is the r-lib example workflow, not a shared one; its deploy uses force: false so it cannot overwrite a badge commit. sanitizers.yml with asan: true joins in Stage 1. Until zufast 0.1.1 is on CRAN, rchk.yml installs it through github-packages.

Small edits get a small run. The shared workflows look at the files a pull request changes, compared with its merge base:

  • Markdown only, such as README.md, NEWS.md or cran-comments.md, skips every check. Only coverage and the pkgdown site run.
  • DESCRIPTION or README.Rmd as well, and nothing else, adds one R CMD check on Ubuntu R-release.
  • Any other file runs everything.

So put a README or DESCRIPTION touch-up in its own pull request. Once a pull request changes code, every later push to it runs every workflow.

Quick by default, full by exception

The full profile is slow. gctorture at step 20 alone has taken 36 to 107 minutes on sibling packages. Waiting on it between roadmap stages was the main thing slowing roadmaps down, so:

  • Pull requests run the quick profile. It should finish in under five minutes. If it doesn’t, raise gctorture’s quick-step or trim quick-containers in the caller workflows; never cut the full profile.
  • A full roadmap stage takes the full-ci label and merges only on a green full run. The roadmap gives the reason in the stage’s **CI.** line, for example first compiled code, a PROTECT or finalizer change, a vendored library, or a Windows-only path.
  • Don’t wait on the full run a merge starts on the default branch, and cancel older full runs it supersedes. A failure that only the full set shows goes on the Full CI stage issue as a comment with the run link, and is fixed there. A failure the quick profile also shows is fixed now.
  • Full CI and v0.1.0 readiness wait for a green full run on their merge commit, and the release commit always needs one.
  • Locally, run gctorture(TRUE) on the code a C change touches when it is cheap; the full run is the authority.

Vendored native code

The design plans to vendor the Arrow C Data Interface header (abi.h) for zu_arrow.c. Nothing is vendored yet; record its licence, pinned version and provenance here when it is.

  • Pin a stable upstream release, never master or a release candidate.
  • Record the tag, the commit and the checksums, and write down the update procedure so the next bump is mechanical.
  • Keep upstream LICENSE and NOTICE under src/vendor/<lib>/, declare the vendored code in DESCRIPTION and inst/COPYRIGHTS.
  • Keep the vendor tree clearly separated from first-party source, and record every local patch and why it exists.
  • CRAN’s compiled-code check applies to vendored code too. No stdout or stderr, no printf, abort, exit or system RNG may be linked, even behind a debug switch that never runs. Remove them with a patch in tools/patches/, list it in src/vendor/PROVENANCE, and make the vendor-verify script check “upstream plus exactly these patches”. Avoid diagnostic-suppressing pragmas too, because they draw their own NOTE. zuhtml is the reference: tools/patches/0002-no-stdio.patch and tools/verify-vendor. zuxml’s first upload was archived because it justified such a symbol instead of patching it.
  • Guard against regressions in CI: run nm -u on the built objects and fail on any of those symbols, so an upstream bump cannot bring them back.

Commits and pull requests

Short, imperative, sentence-case commit subjects, optionally scoped. Keep each commit focused and do not sweep in unrelated files. A pull request explains the user-visible outcome and the rationale, links related issues, lists the checks that were run and the tests that were skipped, and flags platform-sensitive or vendored changes. Performance claims need evidence.

Never commit or push to the default branch. Work on a branch, open a pull request, and leave it for review. Do not merge a pull request unless you are told to.

When you find a defect, in this package or in an upstream tool, open an issue for it rather than only working around it.
